title: Predictive aiming
subtitle: Aim ahead of current motion, then commit to the forecast instead of following the player.
variant: Kern leads Tavi's run with a single committed rune shot
summary: The boss samples the player's movement and aims at an estimated future position, creating a readable invitation to change course.
overview: Tavi runs right while Kern marks a position ahead of the run. At release, the forecast freezes and one rune shot travels along that line. Tavi reverses after commitment, so the shot misses; it does not home. The diagram separates the live player position, forecast, locked trajectory, and projectile hitbox.
learning: Choose a prediction horizon, show what is being forecast, freeze the result, and test a reachable change of course.

demo.title: Inspect the forecast
phaseDescriptions: Tavi moves right. Kern projects a dashed target marker ahead of his current position using the visible direction and speed of travel.
Kern freezes the forecast at the attack cue and releases one projectile along the announced line. Tavi changes direction after commitment; the shot never retargets.
The projectile reaches its forecast destination and disappears. Kern's aiming mark clears before Tavi returns for the next cycle.
demo.danger: Only the moving rune shot has an active hitbox
demo.locked: The forecast and projectile route are fixed at release
demo.safe: Change course after the forecast locks and clear the projectile body
demo.reducedMotion: Autoplay is disabled by reduced-motion settings. Scrub to compare live position, forecast, and shot.
demo.diagramDescription: Tavi runs right while a dashed mark appears ahead of him. Kern locks that forecast and fires one rune shot along the fixed line. Tavi reverses left; the shot passes to the empty forecast point and vanishes.

steps.title: What movement does the boss sample?
steps.body: Use observed position and recent velocity at a defined sample time. Limit the look-ahead interval and clamp the forecast to reachable arena space; do not secretly read future player input.

steps.title: When does the prediction stop changing?
steps.body: Show the forecast marker during aiming, then freeze it at an audible and visible release cue. Spawn the shot on that committed line and keep its velocity fixed unless a separate homing rule is announced.

steps.title: Can an ordinary course change clear it?
steps.body: Test from several approach speeds, distances, and directions. Include the whole player body and projectile radius in clearance checks; leave enough time to reverse or sidestep after the lock.

mistakes.title: Prediction uses hidden future input
mistakes.body: A perfect forecast that reacts to a turn made after commitment feels like input reading. Derive it from a past sample and make any later correction a separately signaled mechanic.

mistakes.title: The marker is too subtle or too late
mistakes.body: If players cannot compare their current position with the projected point before release, the attack reads like an unexplained miss or unavoidable hit. Use geometry and timing, not color alone.

mistakes.title: Lead time outgrows the response window
mistakes.body: An extreme forecast can cover every reachable turn or point beyond the arena. Cap the horizon and test the response at low and high player speeds.

designNotes.title: Predict from data the boss could observe
designNotes.body: Estimate velocity from two recent positions, smooth noise if needed, and compute target = position + velocity × lead time. Make the sample window and lead time explicit tuning parameters.

designNotes.title: Keep forecast and live threat separate
designNotes.body: The dashed marker is a destination cue, not a damage zone. Collision belongs to the moving shot; it should not fire merely because the player touches the future marker.

designNotes.title: Budget motion, not only distance
designNotes.body: Check a standing player, a steady runner, and a runner who reverses just after commitment. Tune projectile travel time and player acceleration together so the intended response stays possible.

designNotes.title: Vary one axis at a time
designNotes.body: Later cycles may shorten the lead time or add a second forecast, but preserve the same lock cue. Combining faster prediction and longer tracking at once hides what changed.

story.title: What the mechanic communicates
story.body: Kern reads the momentum of Tavi's run and stamps a rune where that route would lead. The stone shot obeys the completed mark rather than chasing Tavi's later decision.

adaptation.title: Adapt it to the player verbs
adaptation.body: Tavi needs only ordinary movement to change course after the lock. If a dodge, dash, or guard is added, decide whether it creates a new escape or merely shortens a window that was already fair without it.

distinction.title: Keep the mechanic distinct
distinction.body: Target lock fixes the player's current position; predictive aiming projects from observed movement. Source tracking keeps turning the firing source, while homing changes a projectile after release. This shot does neither once Kern commits.

lensNotes.body: The dashed future marker and release cue expose the projected point before it becomes a committed route.
At release, the sampled velocity, forecast point, and projectile direction stop changing together.
Tavi can reverse after the lock; the escape is a response to a visible prediction, not a hidden random miss.
The marker communicates destination, while only the moving projectile circle participates in collision.
Lead horizon, cue duration, shot travel, and acceleration jointly determine whether a course change is reachable.

examples.body: Squid's boss fight can place spikes and fireworks at positions where it predicts Shelly will be. This forecasts a destination for spawned hazards; Kern's diagram instead commits one traveling shot to a forecast point.

The glint thrown during Sisyphus Prime's Destroy attack attempts to predict the player's position before exploding. It tests a change of momentum under close-range pressure, whereas Kern's shot exposes its entire projected lane.

Rhabdom pressures a moving player with lunges and projectile volleys that reward abrupt grapple-based course changes. The encounter layers several threats around motion prediction; the diagram isolates one forecast and one non-homing projectile.
